title: A bionic robotic trunk with tensegrity-enabled elephant-comparable stiffness variability for assisted daily living

paper_content.abstract: Elephant trunks can rapidly vary their stiffness over a broad range, seamlessly switching between soft states for dexterous operation and rigid states for load-bearing tasks. Despite extensive efforts to mimic this stiffness variability using various approaches, such as jamming structures and phase-change materials, existing bionic robots are limited to narrow tunable stiffness ranges and/or slow switching frequencies. In this work, we present a bionic robotic trunk with a cable-driven tensegrity skeleton, leveraging synergistic and antagonistic muscle-mimicking mechanisms to achieve dynamic stiffness regulation. Through coordinated contraction of motor-actuated cables (i.e., antagonistic action), the robotic trunk achieves a stiffness range of 23.94 to 542.47 N/m and a switching frequency of 1.06 Hz, matching the adaptability of elephant trunks. This rapid and large-scale stiffness variation enables dexterous navigation in unstructured environments and powerful manipulation of heavy objects. Incorporated into an electric wheelchair with the human-machine interface, the robotic trunk assists a post-stroke individual with daily activities, such as opening cabinet doors, retrieving milk from refrigerators, and watering flowers. This work advances bio-inspired robotics and highlights the potential of stiffness-tunable robotic trunks in assistive applications.
paper_content.introduction:
Elephant trunks, with their nearly infinite number of degrees of freedom (DoFs), exemplify an extraordinary balance of dexterity and strength1. Their soft and compliant nature enables delicate tasks such as peeling a banana, while still allowing them to lift loads up to 270 kg2,3. Despite their complex muscular structure, elephant trunks perform rapid, precise movements across diverse tasks, largely thanks to their ability to rapidly modulate stiffness through synergistic and antagonistic muscle actions3,4.

Inspired by this biological marvel, decades of research have focused on developing soft robots mimicking elephant trunks5-9. Currently, three primary approaches are commonly used to realize unique stiffness variability: mechanical locking structures10-12, pneumatic jamming systems13-15, and phase-change materials16-18. Mechanical locking structures utilize body friction or geometric constraint to lock specific configurations, adjusting stiffness for diverse tasks19,20. Pneumatic jamming systems modulate the stiffness by varying the pressure to alter friction between particles, fibers, or layers within fluidic channels21-23. Phase-change materials, such as shape memory alloys (SMAs) and low melting point alloys (LMPAs), exploit temperature-induced phase transition to reversibly change material stiffness24,25. However, each approach has notable limitations26. For example, mechanical locking structures provide only discrete stiffness states, lacking continuous modulation observed in elephant trunks27. Pneumatic jamming systems usually involve bulky external pumps or vacuum sources to adjust the pressure28,29. Phase-change materials, while capable of continuous stiffness changes, suffer from their prolonged actuation cycles, e.g., the notoriously slow cooling process of SMAs30,31.

An alternative strategy, directly inspired by the elephant’s biology, leverages synergistic and antagonistic mechanisms to modulate stiffness32-36. Synergistic mechanisms involve the coordinated contraction/extension of multiple actuators working together to reduce overall stiffness, allowing for soft and compliant motion37. Conversely, antagonistic mechanisms rely on opposing actuator actions that generate counterbalancing forces, rapidly increasing stiffness for loading-bearing tasks27. Although this approach provides a simple and effective means of stiffness modulation without additional complex structures or materials, existing implementations-particularly in cable-driven systems-fail to match the stiffness modulation performance of biological trunks. The primary limitation of existing designs is that their antagonistic actions depend solely on the elastic deformation of actuators-such as cables-while the main structure remains nearly undeformed, resulting in only slight variations in elastic energy and thus a limited stiffness range. For instance, soft continuum robots proposed by Kim et al. exhibited tunable stiffness through synergistic and antagonistic actions of the cables, enhancing adaptive capability for robotic single-port surgery38. However, buckling in the main structure introduces structural instability during antagonistic actions. This instability restricts the large-scale increase in elastic energy, thereby resulting in stiffness that can only be tuned within a narrow range39,40.

In this study, we present a bionic robotic trunk (BRT) that leverages synergistic and antagonistic mechanisms to implement rapid and wide-range stiffness modulation (Fig. 1A). Inspired by the biomechanics of elephant trunks, which modulate internal stiffness through active tensioning of antagonistic muscles to redistribute elastic energy 3, our BRT adopts a cable-driven tensegrity skeleton—a lightweight and compliant architecture that can redistribute elastic energy via cable-induced deformation of struts and springs41,42. Within this skeleton, synergistic actuator contractions enable soft and compliant movements, while antagonistic actions increase stiffness significantly, as showcased in Fig. 1B. Enabled by reconfigurable tensegrity, stored elastic energy is increased by 10 times at antagonistic configuration, yielding stiffness ranging from 23.94 to 542.47 N/m at switching frequency of 1.06 Hz, comparable to that of the elephant trunk (Fig. 1C, Table S1)20,28,37,39,43-53. Subsequently, positional finite element analysis further elucidates the underlying stiffness modulation mechanism. The BRT’s rapid response and broad stiffness range enable it to dynamically adapt to diverse demands and external stimuli. To demonstrate its practical utility, we integrate the BRT into an electric wheelchair with a human-machine interface, showcasing its effectiveness in assisting individuals with daily activities, such as opening cabinet doors, retrieving items from refrigerators, and watering flowers (Fig. 1D). By combing flexibility, strength, and efficiency, the BRT establishes a new benchmark for robotic trunk design, providing a versatile solution for navigating complex environments and assistive robotics.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript presents a cable-driven tensegrity bionic robotic trunk (BRT) that achieves variable stiffness modulation inspired by the muscular architecture of elephant trunks. The system is integrated into an assistive electric wheelchair platform and demonstrates practical utility through real-world user trials.
While the manuscript is clearly written and the engineering effort is commendable, I have concerns regarding the novelty, scientific depth, and generalizability of the work—particularly in the context of Nature Communications. Detailed comments are outlined below.
Major Comments:
1. Limited Novelty in Design and Mechanism
The proposed system combines a cable-driven tensegrity structure, antagonistic actuation, and nonlinear spring-based stiffness modulation. However, all of these elements are based on established techniques in robotics and tensegrity mechanisms, and the manuscript does not present a clearly distinguishable advancement in structural design or mechanism compared to prior work.
Relevant prior work includes (and is recommended for citation):
• [1] Shah DS et al. Tensegrity robotics. Soft Robotics, 2022: A comprehensive review of tensegrity structures for robotic actuation and stiffness control.
These two works present similar designs and mechanisms that utilize tensegrity structures and springs for stiffness modulation:
• [2] Ikemoto S et al. Development of a modular tensegrity robot arm. Frontiers in Robotics and AI, 2021: Demonstrated modular tensegrity arms capable of continuum bending using cable actuation.
• [3] Chen D et al. Bionic tensegrity robotic fish. Biomimetics, 2024: Showcased variable compliance using spring-tethered tensegrity modules for underwater applications.
Given the above, the system lacks a clear advancement in structural principle or mechanism beyond the existing literature.
Additional limitations of the proposed mechanical design include:
• 1.1 Coupling between stiffness and manipulator length: The system modulates stiffness through antagonistic cable pulling, which shortens the entire structure (ΔL). This inherently couples stiffness with posture, limiting independent control of impedance and workspace.
• 1.2 Orientation-dependent gravity compensation: The use of reinforcing springs to maintain alignment appears tuned for a specific mounting configuration. It is unclear how the system performs when mounted vertically or in mobile, orientation-varying applications, raising concerns about generalizability.
• 1.3 Limited adaptability to payload variation: The stiffness adjustment is not dynamically decoupled from geometry or actuation mode, which may reduce robustness in tasks involving variable object dynamics or interactions.
2. Lack of Modeling and Control Contribution
Despite claims of dynamic adaptability and task versatility, the modeling and control aspects of this work remain underdeveloped and do not meet the standards expected for publication in Nature Communications.
2.1 No Control-Theoretic Innovation
• The system operates entirely under open-loop kinematic control using joystick inputs.
• There is no discussion or implementation of dynamic modeling, trajectory planning, impedance/admittance control, or adaptive learning strategies, techniques that are well-established in robotic manipulation.
• The “control model” referenced in Fig. S11 is not formulated mathematically nor validated experimentally.
2.2 No Generalizable Modeling Framework
• The stiffness estimation is based on an empirical analysis of nonlinear spring elongation and elastic energy accumulation. While visually intuitive, this method lacks analytical formulation and does not generalize to other designs or conditions.
• There is no attempt to derive reduced-order models, continuum approximations, or tensegrity statics that would support broader reuse or theoretical insight.
2.3 No Sensor Integration or Feedback
• The robot lacks onboard sensing (e.g., cable tension, force, proprioception, or vision), precluding feedback control or autonomous adaptability.
• This directly contradicts the claims of adaptability and safe interaction (e.g., in the egg-drop test or during human-robot assistance).
• Without sensing and feedback, the system behavior is limited to predefined actuation patterns, with no capacity for reactive decision-making or robustness to uncertainty.
Taken together, these limitations in modeling and control significantly weaken the scientific contribution of the work.
3. Concerns on Application Relevance and Justification
The integration of the BRT into a wheelchair platform with a human–machine interface is well executed and visually compelling. However, the system appears to be developed primarily for demonstration purposes, rather than to address a clearly defined assistive need or user-driven challenge. The work lacks a comparison with alternative solutions, such as existing lightweight robotic arms, which could also be mounted on a wheelchair with similar or better functional outcomes. As such, the superiority or necessity of the proposed system is not convincingly justified.
Minor Comments
• It is also unclear whether long-term reliability concerns, such as cable creep, spring fatigue, or material degradation, have been assessed or mitigated.
• The human evaluation is limited to a single post-stroke participant. Broader user studies or a more systematic assessment would be needed to substantiate the assistive potential of the system.
Conclusion:
While the authors present a well-integrated and experimentally validated robotic platform, the contribution lies primarily in engineering implementation. However, the work exhibits clear limitations in terms of novelty in structural design, the absence of generalizable modeling frameworks, and minimal development in control strategy. These shortcomings render the manuscript, in its current form, unsuitable for publication in Nature Communications.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Nature Comms review
The manuscript under consideration presents a novel cable-driven robotic trunk which leverages tensegrity structures and passive springs to provide continuously-variable stiffness over a large range. Importantly, the tensegrity structure and passive spring configuration is such that although the springs are close to linear, the macroscopic deformation behavior is highly nonlinear, and the variable stiffness is obtained by exploiting this nonlinearity.
The authors describe their trunk design, study its behavior through modeling and a series of experiments, and demonstrate a real-world use case where the trunk is mounted on an electric wheelchair.
The trunk design is novel and highly interesting, thoroughly evaluated with the presented experiments, and the paper is well written.
I have some smaller comments:
* I am missing a description of the overall size/weight of the trunk in the main text. This is important to interpret results such as length change, which is given in cm.
* I am missing a description of how the cable attaches to the frames. Presumably the cables driving the distal portion are anchored at the most distal frame, pass through eyelets in 7 frames, before entering the cable sheath at the 9th frame?
* How does cable friction come into play? Would be pertinent to discuss what effect unmodelled friction would be expected to have on the trunk behavior.
* What is the natural frequency of the trunk for different stiffness configuration? And how does it change with end effector load? One problem frequently arising with soft systems is that they are susceptible to vibrations - is this an issue here? If so, how can it be circumvented? (e.g. you only have springs within the trunk, but no dampers).
* Fig 2: "Reinforcing Spring" label points to sheathed cable; should be pointing to purple spring.
* What is the reason for a 2 x 9 frame configuration? Presumably one could vary both the number of frames per portion and the number of different portions (using 3 cables per portion)?
* It would be useful, though not required, if the authors could provide some intuition regarding the particular design of the tensegrity structure used in the trunk. Which properties are important (e.g. the resultant nonlinear macroscopic behavior)?
* Fig 3 E+F: Is the stiffness a true exponential curve? Or is it just that it is well approximated by an exponential curve? If it is an approximation then I would suggest to make the language more precise. I would find it counterintuitive if linear springs + geometric nonlinearities were to produce an exponential relationship?
* In images/video, I would recommend to make consecutive frames alternating colors, for improved legibility.

Response #1.1
We thank the reviewer for pointing out this important design consideration. We fully acknowledge that the coupling between stiffness modulation and length variation (ΔL) is an inherent trade-off in antagonistic tendon-driven systems. However, this coupling is not merely a limitation—it is also a necessary mechanism to achieve large-scale stiffness modulation. Specifically, without structural shortening, the amount of elastic energy that can be stored through cable antagonism is significantly limited, resulting in only marginal changes in stiffness. In contrast, our design embraces this coupling by enabling the tensegrity skeleton to geometrically shorten under antagonistic loading, thereby increasing internal energy storage and enabling a high stiffness tuning ratio.

To alleviate your concern, we have fully discussed this part in the Discussion. On Page 14,
“One structural trade-off of our stiffness modulation strategy is the coupling between stiffness and manipulator length: antagonistic cable actuation shortens the trunk while increasing its stiffness. This trade-off is intrinsic to many tendon-driven designs, yet crucial—without structural shortening, the elastic energy that can be modulated remains limited, resulting in a narrow stiffness range. In our design, we utilize this shortening behavior to achieve high stiffness ratios, enabled by the geometric reconfiguration of the tensegrity skeleton.
To address workspace concerns, we integrate the BRT into a mobile electric wheelchair platform. The wheelchair’s mobility compensates for any length loss at high stiffness states, allowing the user to reposition the robot as needed and maintain full access to their environment.”

We agree that the stiffness modulation in our design is coupled to the geometry through antagonistic actuation; however, as discussed in Response 1.1, this coupling is an essential mechanism for achieving large-scale stiffness variation. Rather than limiting robustness, it provides the BRT with adaptive mechanical intelligence—allowing the structure to dynamically redistribute tension and stabilize under changing payloads.
We have experimentally validated this adaptability in diverse manipulation scenarios. In the low-stiffness state, the BRT demonstrates excellent shape-morphing ability to navigate and interact safely within cluttered environments (Fig. 3G). Furthermore, to mitigate workspace reduction during high-stiffness configurations, the BRT is integrated into a mobile electric wheelchair platform. The wheelchair’s motion compensates for the geometric shortening that occurs during antagonistic contraction, preserving overall reachability and functional range. This synergy enables the user to perform practical daily tasks such as opening cabinet doors, retrieving items from refrigerators, and watering plants (Fig. 6), illustrating robust real-world adaptability.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Elephant trunks can rapidly vary their stiffness over a broad range, seamlessly switching between soft states for dexterous operation and rigid states for load-bearing tasks. Despite extensive efforts to mimic this stiffness variability using various approaches, such as jamming structures and phase-change materials, existing bionic robots are limited to narrow tunable stiffness ranges and/or slow switching frequencies. In this work, we present a bionic robotic trunk with a cable-driven tensegrity skeleton, leveraging synergistic and antagonistic muscle-mimicking mechanisms to achieve dynamic stiffness regulation. Through coordinated contraction of motor-actuated cables (i.e., antagonistic action), the robotic trunk achieves a stiffness range of 23.94 to 542.47 N/m and a switching frequency of 1.06 Hz, matching the adaptability of elephant trunks. This rapid and large-scale stiffness variation enables dexterous navigation in unstructured environments and powerful manipulation of heavy objects. Incorporated into an electric wheelchair with the human-machine interface, the robotic trunk assists a post-stroke individual with daily activities, such as opening cabinet doors, retrieving milk from refrigerators, and watering flowers. This work advances bio-inspired robotics and highlights the potential of stiffness-tunable robotic trunks in assistive applications.

---

## Introduction

Elephant trunks, with their nearly infinite number of degrees of freedom (DoFs), exemplify an extraordinary balance of dexterity and strength1. Their soft and compliant nature enables delicate tasks such as peeling a banana, while still allowing them to lift loads up to 270 kg2,3. Despite their complex muscular structure, elephant trunks perform rapid, precise movements across diverse tasks, largely thanks to their ability to rapidly modulate stiffness through synergistic and antagonistic muscle actions3,4.

Inspired by this biological marvel, decades of research have focused on developing soft robots mimicking elephant trunks5-9. Currently, three primary approaches are commonly used to realize unique stiffness variability: mechanical locking structures10-12, pneumatic jamming systems13-15, and phase-change materials16-18. Mechanical locking structures utilize body friction or geometric constraint to lock specific configurations, adjusting stiffness for diverse tasks19,20. Pneumatic jamming systems modulate the stiffness by varying the pressure to alter friction between particles, fibers, or layers within fluidic channels21-23. Phase-change materials, such as shape memory alloys (SMAs) and low melting point alloys (LMPAs), exploit temperature-induced phase transition to reversibly change material stiffness24,25. However, each approach has notable limitations26. For example, mechanical locking structures provide only discrete stiffness states, lacking continuous modulation observed in elephant trunks27. Pneumatic jamming systems usually involve bulky external pumps or vacuum sources to adjust the pressure28,29. Phase-change materials, while capable of continuous stiffness changes, suffer from their prolonged actuation cycles, e.g., the notoriously slow cooling process of SMAs30,31.

An alternative strategy, directly inspired by the elephant’s biology, leverages synergistic and antagonistic mechanisms to modulate stiffness32-36. ## Abstract

Elephant trunks can rapidly vary their stiffness over a broad range, seamlessly switching between soft states for dexterous operation and rigid states for load-bearing tasks. Despite extensive efforts to mimic this stiffness variability using various approaches, such as jamming structures and phase-change materials, existing bionic robots are limited to narrow tunable stiffness ranges and/or slow switching frequencies. In this work, we present a bionic robotic trunk with a cable-driven tensegrity skeleton, leveraging synergistic and antagonistic muscle-mimicking mechanisms to achieve dynamic stiffness regulation. Through coordinated contraction of motor-actuated cables (i.e., antagonistic action), the robotic trunk achieves a stiffness range of 23.94 to 542.47 N/m and a switching frequency of 1.06 Hz, matching the adaptability of elephant trunks. This rapid and large-scale stiffness variation enables dexterous navigation in unstructured environments and powerful manipulation of heavy objects. Incorporated into an electric wheelchair with the human-machine interface, the robotic trunk assists a post-stroke individual with daily activities, such as opening cabinet doors, retrieving milk from refrigerators, and watering flowers. This work advances bio-inspired robotics and highlights the potential of stiffness-tunable robotic trunks in assistive applications.

## Introduction

Elephant trunks, with their nearly infinite number of degrees of freedom (DoFs), exemplify an extraordinary balance of dexterity and strength1. Their soft and compliant nature enables delicate tasks such as peeling a banana, while still allowing them to lift loads up to 270 kg2,3. Despite their complex muscular structure, elephant trunks perform rapid, precise movements across diverse tasks, largely thanks to their ability to rapidly modulate stiffness through synergistic and antagonistic muscle actions3,4.

Inspired by this biological marvel, decades of research have focused on developing soft robots mimicking elephant trunks5-9. Currently, three primary approaches are commonly used to realize unique stiffness variability: mechanical locking structures10-12, pneumatic jamming systems13-15, and phase-change materials16-18. Mechanical locking structures utilize body friction or geometric constraint to lock specific configurations, adjusting stiffness for diverse tasks19,20. Pneumatic jamming systems modulate the stiffness by varying the pressure to alter friction between particles, fibers, or layers within fluidic channels21-23. Phase-change materials, such as shape memory alloys (SMAs) and low melting point alloys (LMPAs), exploit temperature-induced phase transition to reversibly change material stiffness24,25. However, each approach has notable limitations26. For example, mechanical locking structures provide only discrete stiffness states, lacking continuous modulation observed in elephant trunks27. Pneumatic jamming systems usually involve bulky external pumps or vacuum sources to adjust the pressure28,29. Phase-change materials, while capable of continuous stiffness changes, suffer from their prolonged actuation cycles, e.g., the notoriously slow cooling process of SMAs30,31.

An alternative strategy, directly inspired by the elephant’s biology, leverages synergistic and antagonistic mechanisms to modulate stiffness32-36. Synergistic mechanisms involve the coordinated contraction/extension of multiple actuators working together to reduce overall stiffness, allowing for soft and compliant motion37. Conversely, antagonistic mechanisms rely on opposing actuator actions that generate counterbalancing forces, rapidly increasing stiffness for loading-bearing tasks27. Although this approach provides a simple and effective means of stiffness modulation without additional complex structures or materials, existing implementations-particularly in cable-driven systems-fail to match the stiffness modulation performance of biological trunks. The primary limitation of existing designs is that their antagonistic actions depend solely on the elastic deformation of actuators-such as cables-while the main structure remains nearly undeformed, resulting in only slight variations in elastic energy and thus a limited stiffness range. For instance, soft continuum robots proposed by Kim et al. exhibited tunable stiffness through synergistic and antagonistic actions of the cables, enhancing adaptive capability for robotic single-port surgery38. However, buckling in the main structure introduces structural instability during antagonistic actions. This instability restricts the large-scale increase in elastic energy, thereby resulting in stiffness that can only be tuned within a narrow range39,40.

In this study, we present a bionic robotic trunk (BRT) that leverages synergistic and antagonistic mechanisms to implement rapid and wide-range stiffness modulation (Fig. 1A). Inspired by the biomechanics of elephant trunks, which modulate internal stiffness through active tensioning of antagonistic muscles to redistribute elastic energy 3, our BRT adopts a cable-driven tensegrity skeleton—a lightweight and compliant architecture that can redistribute elastic energy via cable-induced deformation of struts and springs41,42. Within this skeleton, synergistic actuator contractions enable soft and compliant movements, while antagonistic actions increase stiffness significantly, as showcased in Fig. 1B. Enabled by reconfigurable tensegrity, stored elastic energy is increased by 10 times at antagonistic configuration, yielding stiffness ranging from 23.94 to 542.47 N/m at switching frequency of 1.06 Hz, comparable to that of the elephant trunk (Fig. 1C, Table S1)20,28,37,39,43-53. Subsequently, positional finite element analysis further elucidates the underlying stiffness modulation mechanism. The BRT’s rapid response and broad stiffness range enable it to dynamically adapt to diverse demands and external stimuli. To demonstrate its practical utility, we integrate the BRT into an electric wheelchair with a human-machine interface, showcasing its effectiveness in assisting individuals with daily activities, such as opening cabinet doors, retrieving items from refrigerators, and watering flowers (Fig. 1D). By combing flexibility, strength, and efficiency, the BRT establishes a new benchmark for robotic trunk design, providing a versatile solution for navigating complex environments and assistive robotics.

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript presents a cable-driven tensegrity bionic robotic trunk (BRT) that achieves variable stiffness modulation inspired by the muscular architecture of elephant trunks. The system is integrated into an assistive electric wheelchair platform and demonstrates practical utility through real-world user trials.
While the manuscript is clearly written and the engineering effort is commendable, I have concerns regarding the novelty, scientific depth, and generalizability of the work—particularly in the context of Nature Communications. Detailed comments are outlined below.
Major Comments:
1. Limited Novelty in Design and Mechanism
The proposed system combines a cable-driven tensegrity structure, antagonistic actuation, and nonlinear spring-based stiffness modulation. However, all of these elements are based on established techniques in robotics and tensegrity mechanisms, and the manuscript does not present a clearly distinguishable advancement in structural design or mechanism compared to prior work.
Relevant prior work includes (and is recommended for citation):
• [1] Shah DS et al. Tensegrity robotics. Soft Robotics, 2022: A comprehensive review of tensegrity structures for robotic actuation and stiffness control.
These two works present similar designs and mechanisms that utilize tensegrity structures and springs for stiffness modulation:
• [2] Ikemoto S et al. Development of a modular tensegrity robot arm. Frontiers in Robotics and AI, 2021: Demonstrated modular tensegrity arms capable of continuum bending using cable actuation.
• [3] Chen D et al. Bionic tensegrity robotic fish. Biomimetics, 2024: Showcased variable compliance using spring-tethered tensegrity modules for underwater applications.
Given the above, the system lacks a clear advancement in structural principle or mechanism beyond the existing literature.
Additional limitations of the proposed mechanical design include:
• 1.1 Coupling between stiffness and manipulator length: The system modulates stiffness through antagonistic cable pulling, which shortens the entire structure (ΔL). This inherently couples stiffness with posture, limiting independent control of impedance and workspace.
• 1.2 Orientation-dependent gravity compensation: The use of reinforcing springs to maintain alignment appears tuned for a specific mounting configuration. It is unclear how the system performs when mounted vertically or in mobile, orientation-varying applications, raising concerns about generalizability.
• 1.3 Limited adaptability to payload variation: The stiffness adjustment is not dynamically decoupled from geometry or actuation mode, which may reduce robustness in tasks involving variable object dynamics or interactions.
2. Lack of Modeling and Control Contribution
Despite claims of dynamic adaptability and task versatility, the modeling and control aspects of this work remain underdeveloped and do not meet the standards expected for publication in Nature Communications.
2.1 No Control-Theoretic Innovation
• The system operates entirely under open-loop kinematic control using joystick inputs.
• There is no discussion or implementation of dynamic modeling, trajectory planning, impedance/admittance control, or adaptive learning strategies, techniques that are well-established in robotic manipulation.
• The “control model” referenced in Fig. S11 is not formulated mathematically nor validated experimentally.
2.2 No Generalizable Modeling Framework
• The stiffness estimation is based on an empirical analysis of nonlinear spring elongation and elastic energy accumulation. While visually intuitive, this method lacks analytical formulation and does not generalize to other designs or conditions.
• There is no attempt to derive reduced-order models, continuum approximations, or tensegrity statics that would support broader reuse or theoretical insight.
2.3 No Sensor Integration or Feedback
• The robot lacks onboard sensing (e.g., cable tension, force, proprioception, or vision), precluding feedback control or autonomous adaptability.
• This directly contradicts the claims of adaptability and safe interaction (e.g., in the egg-drop test or during human-robot assistance).
• Without sensing and feedback, the system behavior is limited to predefined actuation patterns, with no capacity for reactive decision-making or robustness to uncertainty.
Taken together, these limitations in modeling and control significantly weaken the scientific contribution of the work.
3. Concerns on Application Relevance and Justification
The integration of the BRT into a wheelchair platform with a human–machine interface is well executed and visually compelling. However, the system appears to be developed primarily for demonstration purposes, rather than to address a clearly defined assistive need or user-driven challenge. The work lacks a comparison with alternative solutions, such as existing lightweight robotic arms, which could also be mounted on a wheelchair with similar or better functional outcomes. As such, the superiority or necessity of the proposed system is not convincingly justified.
Minor Comments
• It is also unclear whether long-term reliability concerns, such as cable creep, spring fatigue, or material degradation, have been assessed or mitigated.
• The human evaluation is limited to a single post-stroke participant. Broader user studies or a more systematic assessment would be needed to substantiate the assistive potential of the system.
Conclusion:
While the authors present a well-integrated and experimentally validated robotic platform, the contribution lies primarily in engineering implementation. However, the work exhibits clear limitations in terms of novelty in structural design, the absence of generalizable modeling frameworks, and minimal development in control strategy. These shortcomings render the manuscript, in its current form, unsuitable for publication in Nature Communications.

Consequently, in the revised manuscript, we highlight cable creep as a current limitation in the Discussion section and identify it as a focus for future work. Additionally, we also discover that stress hysteresis phenomenon occurs in cables after stretching, and this directly impacts the predictive accuracy of theoretical models. However, accurately modeling stress hysteresis in the cables is challenging, since it requires solving complex nonlinear mechanical equations that are difficult to derive and computationally intensive to implement.
